label: section_header
text: Analytical note

label: section_header
text: EVALUATING TRADE MARKS AS A LEADING ECONOMIC INDICATOR OF THE AUSTRALIAN BUSINESS CYCLE

label: text
text: Kevin Nguyen a , Ye Rin Yoo b and Michael Falk a a | IP Australia, b | Allens Patent & Trade Mark Attorneys

label: text
text: For policymakers and businesses, understanding the current state of the economy and where it is headed is crucial for decision making. The most comprehensive measure of economic activity, gross domestic product (GDP), is published with a substantial lag, as are a number of leading economic indicators (LEIs), which predict change in the business cycle.

label: text
text: Increasingly, forecasters and policy makers have sought higher-frequency data sources. IP Australia has an ongoing program of research to understand how intellectual property (IP) data responds to economic shocks and cycles. This analytical note assesses how well trade mark activity in Australia predicts change in Australia's business cycle.

label: section_header
text: At a glance:

label: list_item
text: Trade mark filings provide an early indicator of significant turning points in the business cycle and where the economy is headed in the near term.

label: list_item
text: Compared against 24 key leading economic indicators (LEIs), trade marks rank 6th in their ability to

label: text
text: predict recessionary phases of Australia's business cycle.

label: list_item
text: Based on the study's estimates, a 10% increase in the number of trade marks filed in a given quarter predicts a 2.7% increase in real GDP two quarters after.

label: section_header
text: About the study

label: text
text: The study used quarterly data on the number of trade marks filed in Australia over 5 decades, from Q1 1970 to Q2 2023. Trade marks were identified based on earliest application date. 1 A database was constructed combining this with quarterly time series data for 24 LEIs and quarterly data on Australia's real GDP (see Table A1 in the Appendix for a description of indicators and data sources). Turning points in Australian economic activity were sourced from the Melbourne Institute Phases of the Australian Business Cycle report (2024) 2 . The Melbourne Institute report uses the Bry-Boschan Quarterly rule to determine turning points 3 .

label: section_header
text: Key highlights

label: section_header
text: Trade marks - what are their economic functions?

label: text
text: Trade marks are signs, such as names, logos or other aspects of branding, that indicate the trade origin of goods or services. They have been used for a long time throughout history - from symbols branded on cattle in ancient times 4 to various kinds of branding today. Their core function is to communicate information in the market, most centrally, trade origin, increasing market transparency between producers and consumers. 5 However, they also have other economic functions, including product differentiation, providing a quality guarantee and advertising.6

label: text
text: Businesses can protect their trade marks through 2 legal mechanisms in Australia - depending on whether the trade marks are registered with IP Australia. Unregistered trade marks can be protected at common law by the tort of passing off or under provisions of the Australian Consumer Law7. Registered trade marks are protected under the Trade Marks Act 1995 (Cth). They are also recorded on a register that can be viewed on IP Australia's Australian Trade Mark Search (ATMS) database - which also has an information function8. The Act only recognises 'trade marks' as those that are certain signs and have the core function of indicating trade origin that the courts have coined 'badge of origin'.9 Registration confers exclusive rights to use, and authorise the use of, trade marks and obtain relief from trade mark infringement 10 . It also has benefits, including easier enforcement, transfer of ownership and licensing 11 , and in the valuation of businesses.

label: text
text: Trade marks can rank among the most valuable assets of a business. Firms with stronger growth prospects, better reputation and capacity to commit to higher quality have greater incentive to invest in trade marks. In part, this is because they can spread the fixed marketing costs of developing and protecting trade marks over a larger customer base. 12 In return, trade marks enable firms to differentiate their products from rivals, reducing price competition, and expand into new markets, for example by marketing new products under familiar brands. 13

label: text
text: Businesses typically invest in:

label: list_item
text: new trade marks when they enter a market or launch new goods or services

label: list_item
text: existing trade marks when they expand their goods or services under those trade marks.

label: text
text: As a result, the filings of applications to register trade marks (trade mark filings) can be an indication of the economic conditions that influence business confidence and activity which result in new or expanded trade marks. Whilst registration is only available for certain trade marks and depends on businesses filing their trade marks with IP Australia, this study and other studies have shown a close relationship between trade mark filings and registration and the economy:

label: list_item
text: A study of registered trade marks in the United States found that 60% indicate innovative activity such as new product or service introductions. 14 At the country level, growth in trade mark applications appears linked to increased demand for product variety and quality. 15 Trade mark registrations are also linked to the level of opportunistic entrepreneurship in a country - to start-up activity directed at creating high-growth businesses. 16

label: list_item
text: At the firm level, trade mark filing activity is a significant forward predictor of firm growth. Research by IP Australia estimated that Australian small and medium enterprises (SMEs) that file for a trade mark are 16% more likely to achieve positive employment growth over 3 consecutive years than peers with no recent filings. SMEs that file for patents, trade marks and designs were more than twice as likely to achieve high growth. 17

label: text
text: The current study supports the view that trade mark filings tend to be procyclical, increasing when the economy expands and decreasing when the economy contracts. They provide an early indication of significant turning points in the business cycle and where the economy is heading in the near term.

label: text
text: Trade marks in turn also have an impact on the economy. They increase the flow of information in the market which reduces consumer search costs and business clearance costs and increases economic efficiency. 18 They also drive business innovation, product differentiation and quality which increases competition and productivity. 19

label: section_header
text: Trade marks filing trends and recessions in Australia

label: text
text: In Australia, trade mark filings have generally exhibited an upward trend over the past 5 decades, accounting for seasonal patterns over time. Figure 1 charts the number of trade mark applications filed in each quarter from 1970 to 2023. On average, in the 1970s, around 1,200 applications were filed per quarter, amounting to 4,800 applications per year. By the 2010s, more than 17,000 applications were filed per quarter, totalling over 68,000 applications per year.

label: text
text: Trade mark use is more diffuse throughout the economy than patent use, with sectoral differences in trade mark activity less pronounced than for patents. 20 From the mid-1970 to early 2000s, strong trade mark growth trends have been observed for Australia, the US, the UK and Germany, 21 largely concentrated in services, as well as deregulated and restructured industries. 22

label: text
text: Some of those trends in Australia coincided with significant legislative changes that affected trade mark filings. The spike in 1979 coincided with the amendment to the Trade Marks Act 1955 (Cth) that allowed the registration of trade marks for services in addition to goods. 23 The changes from the mid-1990s to early 2000s coincided with the enactment of the Trade Marks Act 1995 (Cth). 24 The Act broadened 'trade mark' to include more non-traditional signs, 'aspect of packaging, shape, colour, sound or scent'. 25 It also allowed the filing of multi-class applications, except for series trade marks. 26 Jensen and Webster (2004) attributed that to the drop in trade mark filings in 1996 and proposed adjusting trade mark filing data since 1996 upwards by a factor of 1.11 which the present study has adopted. 27 Finally, Australia joined the Madrid System in 2001 and the Act was amended to provide for international registrations. 28

label: text
text: Trade mark filings have also experienced significant fluctuations during key economic downturns including Australia's early 1990s recession, the 2008 Global Financial Crisis and the Covid-19 pandemic. Notably, the Covid-19 shock elicited a counter-cyclical response. Massive demand for goods and services to mitigate the pandemic's impact, and continued availability of finance, drove a trade mark boom throughout 2020 and 2021. The growth was driven largely by repeat trade mark filers diversifying into new goods and services classes, such as surgical and medical apparatus.

label: section_header
text: Turning point analysis

label: text
text: The accuracy of trade mark filings in predicting economic downturns was compared to conventional LEIs using the Quadratic Probability Score (QPS) and Brier's Skill Score (BSS) (Brier, 1950) 29 . These metrics serve as valuable tools for assessing the accuracy of probabilistic predictions of the different phases in the business cycle. A lower QPS and a higher BSS are indicative of indicators that provide more concise estimates of recession phases within the business cycle. Downturns were identified based on quarterly recession periods in the Australian business cycle, provided by the Melbourne Institute report.

label: text
text: The power of trade marks and established LEIs to predict turning points in GDP in the following quarter is reported in the Appendix. Trade marks, when evaluated among 24 LEIs, ranked 6th using QPS score (Table A2) and 7th using BSS score (Table A3) in their ability to predict recession phases in the Australian business cycle based on real GDP. Trade marks had a greater ability than current GDP to predict future GDP. Business confidence index, consumer confidence index, income from sales of goods and services by manufacturers, unemployment rate and retail turnover were among the top 5 predictors of GDP in the next quarter. Counts of Australian businesses and foreign investment in Australia were least predictive of economic down turns.

label: text
text: This result shows that trade mark applications in Australia can serve as a key economic indicator comparable in effectiveness to other traditional LEIs.

label: section_header
text: Time series analysis

label: text
text: Extending on this analysis, a test was undertaken to determine whether there is a fundamental common trend or "cointegration" between trade mark applications and real GDP in Australia. The results of this Engle-Granger test indicated that trade marks and real GDP time series are cointegrated 30 . The relationship between trade marks and real GDP can therefore be assessed through timeseries analysis, with confidence that the estimated relationship is not spurious.

label: text
text: Linear regression model estimates suggest that every 10% increase per quarter in the number of trade mark applications filed in Australia predicts an approximate 1.8% increase in real GDP in the next quarter and a 2.7% increase in real GDP the quarter after. Results of the regression analysis are presented in Table A4 of the Appendix.

label: section_header
text: Significance and future research

label: text
text: IP data is an untapped resource for predicting future economic performance. Innovation is closely aligned with increased productivity and economic growth, however none of the recognised lead economic indicators capture innovative activity. Continuous capture and real time availability gives IP data an advantage over other LEIs. Specifically, in this study we demonstrate the ability of new trade mark filings to predict economic cycles, ranking above other highly regarded indicators such as current gross domestic product and the consumer confidence index.

label: text
text: The study also highlights the importance of the Trade Mark Register as a source of information on the economy. IP Australia and practitioners play a role in assisting businesses to file their trade marks so that they are filed promptly and better reflect market reality. This would strengthen the relationship between trade mark filings and the economy and ensure that trade mark filings continue to be a useful and leading economic indicator.

label: text
text: IP Australia data is publicly accessible on IP Refreshed Automated Product for Information and Data (IP RAPID). IP RAPID provides access to over 100 years of information on IP rights applications. The data covers the 4 forms of registrable IP rights: trade marks, patents, designs and plant breeder's rights.
